Hotels, motels, hospitals, dormitories, all kinds of hospitality-related facilities have majority of their beds small, single sized and the cold Foundation wouldn't? Seems at least odd.

item.title: Re: Possible experimental procedure
item.content:encoded:
Given that this article was submitted in 2009 and the original author hasn't been active since then, I'm not sure if it'd be added.

The article is at the rating it's currently at because of the different standards from 6ish years ago and the time it's had to accumulate those upvotes over the years. Generally nowadays "things that predict fate unerringly" are very hard to write up reasonably because of the experimental designs like the one you've given.

Tl;dr It's a reasonable experiment in-universe, but since the author's not around and this is an old article, it might not be implemented because of the need for substantial new material to be introduced to the article.

item.title: Possible experimental procedure
item.content:encoded:
I propose an expirement to SCP 657.
The expirement will involve one D class subject
The subject will be exposed to SCP 657 and obtain his death timing
However, in the instance of a prediction, D class is to be terminated immediately with prejudice
In the instance of a prediction of immediate termination, D class is to be given a class A amnesiac and guarded in a cell against any possible assault
In the instance of no prediction, D class is to be terminated immediately for security concerns
I'd like to discern if 657 can cause a death, see a death which would not otherwise come about, or is merely predicting a death.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: This one earns a downvote for insufficient testing. If it were even implied that there had been more rigorous testing and what the results were, I might even like it. There are dozens of "fun" experiments to be conducted, starting with killing somebody prematurely, and proceeding on to weirder and weirder stuff, until it ultimately deserves expungement for paradox. Without cautionary warnings, it seems like nobody did any testing except to unwisely cross-test!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I want to like this one, but I'm having a bit of trouble with one element, which nags me constantly as I read it:

Are the subjects of his ability fated to die at the time given, regardless of being informed of that T.O.D.? I'm not a fan of that explanation; it could very well be the case, but it requires no small amount of reality bending, and should be explained further in the article. Or perhaps that is their T.O.D. given that they have been told that that is their T.O.D.? Better, but still probably worthy of some testing logs surrounding it, since I can think of a few ways to mess with that process as well.

I really dislike this one, but it's not for the writing, which is fine. But the concept: Ugh. I just hate the standard boilerplate 'fate' shit that this is referencing. If he could be wrong in his predictions with normal people (but almost always spot on) I think I'd like the implications of that far more. As it stands … I suppose I am downvoting for philosophical reasons, in a way, but I also think this trope is just damn overdone. Plus, he's pretty generic in his creepiness.

Actually on reread I don't know why I got so worked up by that. Shrug.
